Region of interest analyses
For each subject, we assessed the mean T1-signal intensity Z-score
within the areas deﬁned by the following white matter regions
selected as region of interests (ROIs): the ASAF, the uncinate fas-
ciculus, and the white matter corresponding to the aslant tract.

A white matter atlas constructed by Catani et al. (2012) was
consulted to deﬁne the ASAF, ILF, and the uncinate fasciculus.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
PARTICIPANTS
This study included 76 patients (32 female, 73 right-handed) with
chronic aphasia who have undergone language testing and MRI
studies at the University of South Carolina’s Aphasia Lab over a
follow-up period of 10 years.

Individuals were included if they had
a history of one single, left-hemisphere ischemic stroke leading
to neurological symptoms.

MRI DATA COLLECTION
All subjects underwent a structural brain anatomy assessment
using a high-resolution T1-MRI performed at least 6 months after
the stroke, in close chronological proximity with the language
testing session (usually within the same day, but no longer than
1 month apart).

The Pyramids and Palm
Trees Test (Howard and Patterson, 1992) served as a non-verbal
measuretoevaluatesemanticprocessing.

Finally, these intensity values were entered into
a stepwise regression analysis including all six ROIs, along with
lesion size as a control variable (including both cortical and
subcortical damage), to determine which regions remained sig-
niﬁcant predictors for each behavioral measure, given extent of
damage and damage to all other areas as cofactors.

Thus, the threshold
for signiﬁcance was set to p = 0.025.

Although T1-signal intensity is an indirect
measure of tissue integrity (and is correlated with T2 hyperin-
tensities, also an indirect measure of white matter integrity), T1
images were used as due to better tissue contrast, these scans facil-
itate more speciﬁc regional assessment of damage.

source_passages.quote:
Three simultaneous multiple linear
regression analyses were conducted to determine if years of education and aphasia
severity (defined by WAB-AQ score) were predictive of reading performance for
the 67 PWA with alexia on reading performance for all word types, for perfor-
mance on real-word reading, and then for performance on pseudohomophones
and nonwords.

Performance on WAB-AQ had a unique, positive effect on total reading, lexical
reading, and sublexical reading.

Holding years of education constant, the models
predicted for every one-point increase on WAB-AQ, there is an expected 0.7%
increase on total reading score, p < .001, sr2 = .57, effect size; an expected 0.9%
increase on lexical reading, p < .001, sr2 = .57; and an expected 0.3% increase on
sublexical reading, p < .001, sr2 = .30.

Education, on the other hand, was not
uniquely predictive of total reading, lexical reading, or sublexical reading, p = .07,
p = .14, p = .06, respectively.

The inclusion criteria for PWA were history of left hemisphere stroke at least 6
months prior to enrolment and a diagnosis of aphasia confirmed by a licenced
speech–language pathologist based on an aphasia quotient (AQ) of less than 93.8/
1466
BROOKSHIRE ET AL.

The average months
poststroke onset was 70.55 (SD = 54.99).

We employed a retrospective analysis of a convenience sample of indivi-
duals with chronic aphasia that may not have been fully representative of the
population with stroke-associated aphasia at large, despite our inclusion of indivi-
duals with a range of aphasia types and severity, and despite the fact that type of
aphasia and alexia was not a criterion for inclusion.

The inclusion of a wide range of
aphasia types and severity was potentially problematic given that some individuals in
this sample were likely to present with cooccurring motor speech impairments, which
could have negatively impacted oral reading performance.

Three simultaneous multiple linear
regression analyses were conducted to determine if years of education and aphasia
severity (defined by WAB-AQ score) were predictive of reading performance for
the 67 PWA with alexia on reading performance for all word types, for perfor-
mance on real-word reading, and then for performance on pseudohomophones
and nonwords.

Performance on WAB-AQ had a unique, positive effect on total reading, lexical
reading, and sublexical reading.

Education, on the other hand, was not
uniquely predictive of total reading, lexical reading, or sublexical reading, p = .07,
p = .14, p = .06, respectively.

The inclusion criteria for PWA were history of left hemisphere stroke at least 6
months prior to enrolment and a diagnosis of aphasia confirmed by a licenced
speech–language pathologist based on an aphasia quotient (AQ) of less than 93.8/
1466
BROOKSHIRE ET AL.

The average months
poststroke onset was 70.55 (SD = 54.99).

We employed a retrospective analysis of a convenience sample of indivi-
duals with chronic aphasia that may not have been fully representative of the
population with stroke-associated aphasia at large, despite our inclusion of indivi-
duals with a range of aphasia types and severity, and despite the fact that type of
aphasia and alexia was not a criterion for inclusion.

Regarding the stimuli employed, this study is limited by the fact that only oral
reading abilities for single words were assessed, and this work does not speak to text
comprehension abilities in PWA and alexia.

Similarly, articulation of words with a high

travel, t(32) ¼ 3.24, p < .01 (M ¼ 26% vs 20%, respectively).

Participants
The study included 33 patients (27 males) who had a history of
a single, left hemisphere stroke.

Other study criteria included
that patients be right-handed and native English speakers, with
no prior history of psychiatric or neurologic disorders.

This test required patients to repeat an auditorily-pre-
sented word ﬁve times in succession.

Half of the words had a low degree of travel (i.e., the
consonants were in a similar place of articulation, e.g., nicety),
and the other half, a high degree of travel (e.g., tobacco).

The
low-travel condition consisted of words ranging between zero
travel (e.g., sanity) and one place transition (e.g., ﬂattery), while
the high-travel condition included words with one, two (e.g.,
tobacco), and three place transitions (e.g., spaghetti).

It is important to note, however, that participants were
tested in the post-acute phase of stroke, when both lesion site
and behavioral proﬁle were relatively stable.

source_passages.quote:
Content analyses conducted on all connected speech samples indicated
that performance differed across discourse genres and between groups.

Speciﬁcally, storytelling narratives provided higher quanti-

Materials and methods
Participants
Forty-six patients who had developed aphasia following a single
left haemorrhagic or ischaemic stroke were tested in the chronic
stage (412 months post-stroke).

Discourse samples
Three discourse samples were collected from each participant
with no time limit: (i) descriptive discourse, elicited using the
‘Cookie Theft’ composite picture from the BDAE (Goodglass
and Kaplan, 1983); (ii) narrative discourse, elicited using a
‘Dinner Party’ storytelling script (Fletcher and Birt, 1983), which
involved a series of eight black-and-white sequences of pictures;
and (iii) unsupported procedural discourse, which was elicited
by asking participants to describe ‘how they prepare a cup of
tea’.

For quantity of produc-
tion, storytelling narrative was significantly higher than both
composite
picture
description
and
procedural
discourse
(P5 0.001).

For lexical diversity, storytelling was again the
highest, followed by composite picture description and then
procedural discourse.

Finally, for speech rate,
the fastest speech was produced during procedural discourse,
followed by picture description, and then storytelling.

source_passages.quote:
Materials and methods
Participants
Forty-six patients who had developed aphasia following a single
left haemorrhagic or ischaemic stroke were tested in the chronic
stage (412 months post-stroke).

Discourse samples
Three discourse samples were collected from each participant
with no time limit: (i) descriptive discourse, elicited using the
‘Cookie Theft’ composite picture from the BDAE (Goodglass
and Kaplan, 1983); (ii) narrative discourse, elicited using a
‘Dinner Party’ storytelling script (Fletcher and Birt, 1983), which
involved a series of eight black-and-white sequences of pictures;
and (iii) unsupported procedural discourse, which was elicited
by asking participants to describe ‘how they prepare a cup of
tea’.

First, the number of content words was counted as a measure of
quantity of production.

Second, the number of distinct
content words (type count) was coded as a measure of lexical
diversity.

Finally, words per minute (WPM) measur-
ing speech rate was obtained by dividing the total number of
tokens by the duration of the sample.

These analyses were repeated, but in-
stead, the between-subject group factor involved fluent (n = 25)
versus non-fluent (n = 21) aphasia groups, the patients were
grouped according to their aphasia classification as diagnosed
using the BDAE and demonstrated in Table 1.

There were
significant main effects of discourse genre for quantity of
production [F(2,88) = 45.18, P 5 0.001, partial g2 = 0.51],
lexical diversity [F(2,88) = 62.84, P5 0.001, partial g2 =
0.59], and speech rate [F(2,88) = 5.01, P = 0.009, partial g2
= 0.1].

A greater number of words were produced during
storytelling narrative than picture description and procedural
discourse (P 5 0.001).

For lexical diversity, there was greater
diversity during storytelling followed by picture description
and then procedural discourse.

The differences were signifi-
cant between storytelling and the other two discourses
(P 5 0.001), and between picture description and procedural
discourse (P = 0.01).

Finally, for speech rate, patients spoke
significantly faster during procedural discourse compared to
both storytelling and picture description (P 4 0.003).

The differences between the two groups were sig-
nificant for all three discourses with better performance
among the fluent group (P 5 0.001).

A statistical inferencing, one-stage, random effects, network meta-analysis

comprehension, naming, and functional communication pre-post intervention gains, adjusting for a priori–defined covariates 
(age, sex, time poststroke, and baseline aphasia severity), reporting estimates of mean change scores (95% CI).
RESULTS: Data from 959 individual participant data (25 trials) were included.

We confirmed baseline and subse-
quent time point data extraction and sought unreported data 
from the primary researchers where possible.9a,18
For each language outcome, we identified the outcome mea-
surement most frequently used by included data sets (anchor 
measure) and transformed the remainder (minority measures) 
to match the anchor’s range and format, thus retaining a clini-
cally meaningful change from baseline score as a measure of 
effect size.18 Anchor measure overall language scores were 
represented by the Western Aphasia Battery–Aphasia Quotient 
(WAB-AQ), auditory comprehension was represented by 
the Aachen Aphasia Test–Token Test (AAT-TT), naming by the 
Boston Naming Test, and functional communication by the 
Aachen Aphasia Test–Spontaneous Speech Communication 
(AAT-SSC) rating score.21
Data on SLT interventions were categorized by regimen (fre-
quency, intensity, duration, and dosage), content (home practice, 
theoretical approach, language target, individualized tailoring by 
functional relevance, or difficulty level), delivery (face to face, 
computer supported, or self-managed), setting (in/outpatient), 
and provider (professional/nonprofessional).18,21 We cross-
checked data with primary research teams and available docu-
mentation.

errors on the 5 repetitions, it was scored as a single error).

quency, intensity, duration, and dosage), content (home practice,

functional relevance, or difficulty level), delivery (face to face, 
computer supported, or self-managed), setting (in/outpatient),

mentation.

acy of different types of complex structures also differed: sen­

and passives did not differ statistically (estimate: −0.29, SE: 
0.36, Z = −0.11, P = 0.42).

Materials and methods
Participants and measures
Participants included 131 individuals (32 females and 99 
males) who sustained a single left hemisphere stroke at least 
6 months before being tested and scanned.

Behavioural data
Participants’ language performance was evaluated with the 
Curtiss–Yamada Comprehensive Language Evaluation 
(CYCLE-R55) test.

Statistical analysis
Behavioural
Patients’ auditory comprehension accuracy on the CYCLE-R 
was analysed with logit mixed-effect models,67
with 
Sentence Group as a fixed effect, and random intercepts for 
the subject grouping factor.68 Potential inter-relationships 
among the comprehension of different sentence types were 
assessed using Pearson correlations.

The current study utilized the CYCLE-R, which was devel­
oped to test comprehension on a wide range of syntactic 
structures but has a small number of test stimuli per subtest 
and a non-exhaustive set of sentence types.

Also, although 
the CYCLE-R controls for a number of linguistic variables 
across sentence types (e.g. word frequency), other variables 
are not controlled (e.g. sentence length), thus limiting the 
ability of creating controlled minimal pairs.9 Another limita­
tion is that our disconnection analyses relied on indirect 
measures of structural disconnection, as diffusion tensor im­
aging data were only available for a subset of participants.

To explore the lack of word class eﬀect
further, word class along with other linguistic variables (imageability,
frequency, age-of-acquisition, familiarity, world length and visual
complexity) were entered into a multiple regression analysis to
predict naming accuracy in post-stroke aphasia.

The regression model
was
signiﬁcant
(R2 = 0.04,
F(1,128) = 5.23,
p = 0.024),
with
imageability appearing as the only signiﬁcant predictor (B = 1.78,
t = 2.29, p = 0.024).

These results conﬁrmed the lack of
word class eﬀect (once imageability and other factors are controlled)
for the production and comprehension of single-words in post-stroke
aphasia, as word class did not appear to be a signiﬁcant predictor in
both analyses.

ho-cort_44.basis: Legacy entry for HarvardOxford cortical label 44 region (IFG pars opercularis, BA 44); the entry is the left one.

left_anterior_arcuate_fasciculus.basis: The anterior segment (Catani et al. 2005) links the inferior frontal and inferior parietal cortex: in XTRACT, SLF III.

left_anterior_temporal_lobe.basis: Anterior temporal lobe as the entry defines it (aliases ATL, temporal pole) = temporal pole with the anterior superior and middle temporal gyri.

left_anterior_temporal_lobe__Robson2014.basis: Robson et al. 2014 region; its aliases add the anterior fusiform gyrus to the anterior temporal lobe.

left_arcuate_fasciculus_slf.basis: The entry combines the arcuate and the SLF ("dorsal language pathway"), so XTRACT's arcuate and JHU's SLF.

left_dorsolateral_prefrontal_cortex.basis: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (BA 9/46) lies mainly on the middle frontal gyrus; the atlases have no DLPFC label.

left_dorsomedial_prefrontal_cortex.basis: The dorsomedial prefrontal cortex is the medial superior frontal gyrus (AAL Frontal_Sup_Medial).

left_inferior_frontal_occipital_fascicul.basis: Spelling variant of the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus.

left_long_segment_arcuate_fasciculus.basis: The long (direct fronto-temporal) segment is part of XTRACT's arcuate, which does not separate the segments.

left_occipito_temporal_sulcus.basis: The occipito-temporal sulcus has no atlas label; it separates the inferior temporal and fusiform gyri, whose temporo-occipital parts are used.

left_parietal_association_cortex.basis: Parietal association cortex = inferior parietal lobule (supramarginal, angular) and superior parietal lobule.

left_posterior_arcuate_fasciculus.basis: The posterior (temporo-parietal) segment has no XTRACT label; XTRACT's arcuate is the closest tract.

left_posterior_middle_temporal_gyrus.basis: Same structure (the temporo-occipital part is not included).

left_posterior_planum_temporale_spt.basis: Area Spt lies in the posterior planum temporale, which the atlases do not subdivide.

left_precentral_gyrus_insula.basis: The "precentral gyrus of the insula" (Dronkers 1996, apraxia of speech) is the superior precentral gyrus OF THE INSULA, not the motor precentral gyrus; the atlases do not subdivide the insula, so the whole insula is used.

left_premotor_cortex.basis: Premotor cortex (BA 6) has no atlas label; it spans the anterior precentral gyrus laterally and the supplementary motor area medially.

left_rolandic_operculum.basis: The Rolandic operculum is HarvardOxford's central opercular cortex.

left_superior_temporal_gyrus.basis: Whole superior temporal gyrus (aliases name both anterior and posterior parts).

left_superior_temporal_gyrus__Leff2009.basis: Leff et al. 2009 region (aliases posterior STG, posterior superior temporal sulcus, planum temporale); the sulcus has no atlas label.

left_superior_temporal_gyrus_wernicke.basis: Wernicke's area as the entry defines it (aliases: posterior STG, planum temporale).

left_superior_temporal_sulcus.basis: The superior temporal sulcus has no atlas label; it lies between the superior and middle temporal gyri, whose posterior divisions are used.

left_supramarginal_gyrus_premotor.basis: The entry groups the supramarginal gyrus with the inferior postcentral gyrus (aliases).

left_temporal_lobe.basis: All lateral and basal temporal units.

left_temporal_pole_mtg.basis: Middle temporal part of the temporal pole (AAL Temporal_Pole_Mid).

left_temporal_pole_stg.basis: Superior temporal part of the temporal pole (AAL Temporal_Pole_Sup).

left_temporobasal__Goldenberg1994.basis: Basal temporal cortex (Goldenberg 1994) = inferior temporal and fusiform gyri.

left_temporoparietal_junction.basis: The temporoparietal junction has no atlas label; taken as the posterior superior temporal, posterior supramarginal and angular gyri.

right_lateral_frontal_cortex.basis: Lateral frontal cortex taken as the inferior and middle frontal gyri.

right_medial_frontal_cortex.basis: Medial frontal cortex = HarvardOxford frontal medial cortex plus the medial superior frontal gyrus.

right_middle_temporal_gyrus.basis: Whole middle temporal gyrus, right hemisphere.

right_posterior_perisylvian_cortex.basis: Posterior perisylvian cortex taken as the posterior superior temporal gyrus, planum temporale and supramarginal gyrus.

angular_gyrus.basis: HarvardOxford label of the same structure.
angular_gyrus.name: Angular gyrus

arcuate_fasciculus.basis: XTRACT label of the same tract (the whole arcuate; its segments are not separated).
arcuate_fasciculus.name: Arcuate fasciculus

central_operculum.basis: HarvardOxford's central opercular cortex is the Rolandic operculum.
central_operculum.name: Central (Rolandic) operculum

forceps.basis: Midline labels without a side in JHU, so the side is taken from the lesion voxels. JHU labels only the anterior and posterior callosal radiations (forceps minor, major), not the callosal body; a lesion in the body is not measured.

paracingulate_gyrus.basis: HarvardOxford label of the same structure.

putamen.basis: Not in the cortical HarvardOxford atlas; AAL label of the same structure.

slf.basis: JHU's superior longitudinal fasciculus label (the fronto-parietal body of the SLF).
slf.name: Superior longitudinal fasciculus (fronto-parietal part)

slf_iii.basis: XTRACT label of the same tract; SLF III links the inferior frontal gyrus with the supramarginal gyrus.

unmapped.left_extreme_capsule: No atlas used here (JHU, XTRACT) labels the extreme capsule. It carries the inferior fronto-occipital and uncinate fasciculi, but those tracts are not the extreme-capsule fibre system itself, so it is not approximated.
unmapped.left_frontal_white_matter_bottleneck: A "bottleneck" is a region defined in its source paper by the convergence of several tracts, not an atlas structure.
unmapped.left_perisylvian_network: A network, not a single anatomical structure.
unmapped.left_posterior_middle_temporal_white_mat: White matter under the posterior middle temporal gyrus; no tract label.

coverage.need: The inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus has 3 findings; the anterior thalamic radiation (measured by JHU) none. Both were linked to semantic deficits and verbal fluency in stroke cohorts that measured tract damage directly.
3 findings on the inferior temporal gyrus and 5 on the fusiform gyrus, regions often damaged by posterior cerebral artery strokes and relevant to naming and reading.

7 findings, but neither JHU nor XTRACT labels the extreme capsule. Oeckel et al. 2021 and Kümmerer et al. 2013 measured it with tractography-derived templates from healthy subjects; extracting them documents the ventral-stream evidence, and their templates (if shared) would make the region reachable.

3 findings on the supplementary motor area and 1 on the frontal aslant tract (reachable since the XTRACT atlas was added), which connects it to the inferior frontal gyrus and is linked to verbal fluency after stroke.

The insula's role in apraxia of speech rests mainly on Dronkers 1996 (precentral gyrus of the insula) and is disputed: Hillis et al. 2004 placed it in the posterior inferior frontal gyrus instead. The frontal operculum has no finding at all. Both sides should be in the KB.
Every right-hemisphere region has 1-3 findings. Right-hemisphere structure and its role in recovery matter for interpreting a left-hemisphere lesion (and for right-hemisphere or bilateral lesions).

Lesions often reach the thalamus, caudate, putamen and pallidum (AAL measures all four), but the KB has no finding on the thalamus or caudate and 4 findings from one paper on putamen and pallidum (Radanovic & Mansur 2017 was extracted as a narrative review, without region-level findings). The subcortical-aphasia literature also shows that much of it reflects cortical hypoperfusion, which the report should be able to say.
